edits.english: The Gemara asks with regard to Abaye’s reasoning: Is this to say that the halakhot of pure items are more stringent than those concerning libation wine? The Gemara answers: Indeed, that is so. As it was stated that there was a dispute with regard to a courtyard whose owners divided it among themselves with a low partition (meseifas). Rav says: If one’s neighbor on the other side of the partition is an am ha’aretz, his pure items that he leaves in the courtyard are rendered impure, but in the case of a gentile neighbor, Rav says this does not render the Jew's wine an idolatrous libation. And Rabbi Yoḥanan says: The pure items remain pure as well. Evidently, Rav considers the halakhot of purity more stringent than those of libation wine.

edits.hebrew: למימרא דטהרות אלימי מיין נסך – מדנקט לה בלשון קל וחומר.
שחלקה במסיפס – מחיצה נמוכה, עם הארץ מצד זה, וחבר שטהר טהרות מצד זה.
אינו עושה יין נסך – דנתפס עליו כגנב. אלמא, טהרות אלימי.

edits.english: They question the very assumption in Abaye's words: Is this to say that pure items are more stringent than libation wine? They answer: Indeed, as it was stated that they disagreed on this matter: A courtyard whose owners divided it with a *meseifas*, a thin, small barrier less than ten handbreadths high. Rav says: If there was an *am ha'aretz* on the other side, the *haver*'s pure items in the other part of the courtyard are impure. But if there was a gentile on the other side, the gentile does not render the wine a libation. And Rabbi Yoḥanan says: The pure items remain pure as well. In any case, we see from here that according to Rav's view, they are more stringent regarding pure items than they are concerned about libation wine.

A *meseifas* is a small partition that is not ten handbreadths high. It serves to define each person's part in the courtyard, but it is not considered a complete partition such that the neighbor would be accused of being a thief if he enters the other side of the partition (see *Bava Batra* 6b). Therefore, regarding libation wine, since even the gentile knows that this part of the courtyard belongs to his fellow, the gentile is ashamed to enter there. For this reason, if we did not see the gentile there, we do not suspect that he touched the wine. However, if it is known that he entered there, there is a concern, since he would not be accused of being a thief. This is not the case for pure items, which are impure in any case since he would not be accused of being a thief (Ra'avad).

The Ramban (and several other early authorities) summarize that there are four main different laws regarding this matter. The first case is when the gentile has no connection to the wine or to the house where the wine is located. In this case, even if the gentile is found standing next to the wine, there is no concern that he touched it. The second case is when the gentile has a connection to the wine but not to the house. If the gentile is found next to the wine, there is a concern that he touched it. The third case is when the gentile has a connection to the house (or has permission to be there) but not to the wine. There is a concern for the wine unless it was guarded, or the wine was locked or sealed. The fourth case is when the gentile has permission for both the wine and the house. In this situation, the wine is only permitted if there were Jews constantly watching the gentile and ensuring he did not touch it.

In a courtyard divided by a *meseifas* (a light fence), with a *haver* on one side and an *am ha'aretz* on the other side, the *haver*'s pure items are pure even if the *am ha'aretz*'s hand can reach there, because they are in the *haver*'s domain. If there was a gentile on one side and an Israelite on the other side, and there was a *meseifas* between them, even if the gentile's hand reaches the Israelite's portion, there is no concern for libation wine or for pure items. This is in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan's words (Rambam *Sefer Tahara*, *Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav* 12:21; *Sefer Kedusha*, *Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot* 13:7; *Shulchan Arukh*, *Yoreh De'a* 129:16).

Early commentators offer several interpretations for this word, and there is no certainty regarding its origin, which is certainly from a foreign language. Some believe (R.B.) that its origin is in Greek *mesoporos*, meaning something hollow in its middle, which aligns with the Geonim's interpretation that a *meseifas* is a wall full of windows. Others say its origin is in Latin *sepes*, meaning a fence or partition, or in Greek *psephos*. However, it is likely related to the Greek root *mesos*, meaning middle, something that stands in between.

The Gemara raises an objection to Rav's opinion from a *baraita*: If the inner courtyard belongs to a ḥaver, i.e., one devoted to the meticulous observance of *mitzvot*, especially the *halakhot* of purity, *terumah*, and tithes, and the outer courtyard to an am ha’aretz, that ḥaver may lay out his produce there, in the inner courtyard, and place his vessels there, without concern that the *am ha'aretz* will touch the produce and vessels and render them impure. And this applies even if the hand of the am ha’aretz can reach there. This poses a difficulty to Rav's opinion, who holds that even in a situation with a partition, there is concern about contact with an *am ha'aretz*.

edits.hebrew: מיתיבי – שתי חצרות זו לפנים מזו, הפנימית של חבר.
וחיצונה – הפתוחה לרשות הרבים, של עם הארץ, דאין לו לעם הארץ דריסת הרגל על הפנימית.
שוטח שם – בפנימית. אבל אי הוי איפכא, דחיצונה של חבר, כיון דהוי לעם הארץ דריסת הרגל בחיצונה, אין חבר שוטח שם פירותיו. מכל מקום, קשיא לרב, דקתני: אף על פי שידו של עם הארץ מגעת לשם.

edits.english: Regarding Rav's view concerning pure items, they raise an objection from what we learned: There were two courtyards, one inside the other. The inner courtyard belonged to a *haver* who was meticulous in the laws of purity, and the outer courtyard belonged to an *am ha'aretz* who was not meticulous in them. That *haver* may lay out produce and place vessels there in the inner courtyard, even if the *am ha'aretz*'s hand can reach there. If so, this is a difficulty for Rav's opinion, for even in a place with a division and a partition, he is concerned about the *am ha'aretz*'s touch!

The Gemara answers that Rav could say to you: It is different there, as the *am ha'aretz* would be caught and accused as a thief if he were to tamper with the produce, as the *am ha'aretz* has no business being in the inner courtyard. Therefore, there is no concern that the *am ha'aretz* will tamper with the produce.

edits.hebrew: התם משום דנתפס עליו כגנב – דמה לו בפנימית? אבל חלוקה, דכחצר אחד דמי, כי עייל ידיה לא מתפיס כגנב.

edits.english: They answer: Rav could say to you: It is different there, as the *am ha'aretz* would be caught as a thief. For in the inner courtyard, the *am ha'aretz* has no business at all, and if he enters there, he is considered a thief. Therefore, we do not suspect that he would do so.

The Gemara suggests: Come and hear support for Rav’s opinion from a *baraita* (Tosefta, *Teharot* 9:11): Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: If the roof of a ḥaver is above the roof of his neighbor who is an am ha’aretz, that ḥaver may lay out produce there and place vessels there, provided that the hand of the am ha’aretz cannot reach the haver's roof; but if it is within the *am ha'aretz*'s reach, the *haver*'s pure items are rendered impure. This poses a difficulty to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who deems pure items permitted in a courtyard divided by a low partition.

They propose: Come and hear a proof for Rav's opinion from what we learned: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: If the roof of a *haver* is above the roof of an *am ha'aretz*, that *haver* may lay out produce and place vessels there, provided that the hand of the *am ha'aretz* cannot reach the *haver*'s roof. For if the *am ha'aretz*'s hand can reach, the *haver*'s pure items are impure. If so, this is a difficulty for Rabbi Yoḥanan, who permitted pure items in a courtyard divided by a *meseifas*!

If the roof of a *haver* is above the roof of an *am ha'aretz*, the *haver* may lay out his vessels and his pure produce there, and they retain their status even if the *am ha'aretz* can reach out his hand to touch them. This applies to a gentile as well, if the Jew's courtyard is above the gentile's, and he need not be concerned either with regard to impurity or with regard to libation wine. This is in accordance with the opinion of the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (Rambam *Sefer Tahara*, *Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav* 12:19 and *Kesef Mishne* there).

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you: It is different there, as the *am ha'aretz* has a way to excuse his behavior if he were to be discovered reaching up to the upper roof, by saying: I merely stretched myself; I was not intending to tamper with anything.

edits.hebrew: אמצרי – דגג קמצרנא, אני מכוון למדת בניין שאני רוצה למדוד, לכך הושטתי את ידי. לשון אחר מתשובת הגאונים: מתמוגג אני, אשטנדלינ"ר בלע"ז, וגרסינן: אימצודי קא ממצדנא.

edits.ref: Otzar Laazei Rashi, Talmud, Avodah Zarah 147
edits.english:
1910 / (Avodah Zarah 70b) / *Imtzurei ka mimtzara*
Estendeillier: to stretch, to extend / [estendeillier] estendeilier
The foreign word appears after "Another interpretation: I am stretching myself," and refers to the movements of a person lying lazily and stretching their limbs for pleasure. The manuscript reads "mitmoded," which can also be interpreted as "stretching oneself," meaning to extend the limbs to their full length. Additionally, Rashi brings another version "imtzudi ka mimtzadna," apparently "I am turning on my side," and this also indicates an unintentional movement of the limbs.
✭ to stretch

They answer: Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you: It is different there, as the *am ha'aretz* has a way to excuse himself if he is found reaching his hand to the upper roof. He would say: I only want to stretch myself, and that is why I raised my hand, but I did not intend to do anything.

Come and hear what is taught in that same *baraita*: If the roof of a ḥaver is beside the roof of an am ha’aretz, that ḥaver may lay out produce there and place vessels there, even if the hand of the am ha’aretz can reach the haver's roof. This poses a difficulty to Rav's statement. The Gemara answers that Rav could say to you: Isn’t there the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, which aligns with my opinion with regard to roofs that are next to one another? What I say is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion.

edits.hebrew: בצד גגו – שאינו גבוה ממנו, וליכא למימר: מתמוגג אני כשמושיט ידו שם.
אנא דאמרי כרשב"ג – דאמר לעיל: ובלבד שלא תהא ידו של עם הארץ מגעת שם. ולרב לא שני ליה בין שגג חבר למעלה בין שהוא שווה לו.

edits.english: They propose: Come and hear a proof from what we learned: If the roof of a *haver* is beside the roof of an *am ha'aretz*, that *haver* may lay out produce and place vessels there, even if the *am ha'aretz*'s hand can reach the *haver*'s roof. This is a difficulty for Rav! They answer: Rav could say to you: Is there not the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel which aligns with my view regarding adjacent roofs? What I say is in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion.

If the roof of a *haver* is beside or lower than the roof of an *am ha'aretz*, any place where the *am ha'aretz* can reach out and touch is presumed to be impure, in accordance with the statement of the first *tanna* in the *Tosefta*. With regard to a gentile, the Rambam says that if there is a low partition between them, the Jew need not be concerned with regard to either libation wine or impurity (Rambam *Sefer Tahara*, *Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav* 12:19 and *Kesef Mishne* there, and *Sefer Kedusha*, *Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot* 13:7; *Shulchan Arukh*, *Yoreh De'a* 129:16).
